Civil engineers across the region spent the spring reviewing the water system, and their report, released to councillors last month, described a network that had aged unevenly. The oldest mains, laid before 1900, still served several neighbourhoods, while newer districts relied on pipes installed after reconstruction. Inspectors walked miles of service roads, recorded every leak they could find, and photographed corroded joints. Some residents complained about brown water; others reported nothing at all. The council asked three firms to bid on repairs, held two public meetings, and promised a decision before winter.

Funding remained the hardest question. Federal grants covered less than half the projected cost, and the state had already committed its share to other projects. Officials considered raising rates, issuing bonds, or delaying the least urgent work. Each option carried political risk, and the mayor, facing an election that autumn, refused to endorse any of them publicly. Behind the scenes, however, her staff drafted a phased plan that would spread spending across a decade.

The technical review itself was thorough. Teams surveyed every valve and hydrant, tested pressure at more than two hundred points, and logged the results in a shared database. They found that the eastern reservoir, built in 1954, had begun to silt up, and that two booster stations relied on pumps long past their service lives. A consulting firm ran hydraulic models for three demand scenarios and concluded that the network would fail to meet peak summer demand within five years unless the most troubled segments were replaced.

Not everyone trusted the models. A retired engineer, who had worked for the city for thirty-one years, argued that the assumptions about population growth were too optimistic and that the consultants had underestimated the expense involved in traffic disruption. She pointed out that the failure of the eastern pump during the heat wave two summers ago had forced the city to truck in water for eleven days, and she warned that a similar breakdown in a denser neighbourhood could be far worse. Her comments, appended to the official record, prompted the council to request an independent audit.

The audit team reviewed the same data and reached a similar conclusion, though it proposed a different sequence of repairs. Rather than starting with the eastern reservoir, it recommended replacing the distribution mains first, since those pipes served the most households and had the highest failure rate. The team also urged the city to build a second intake on the river, arguing that redundancy mattered more than capacity. Council members debated the trade-offs for weeks, and the final budget, approved by a narrow margin, combined elements of both plans.
